MY PROVENANCE FIX WAS UNSOUND: RE-PINNING RESTORES THE PATCH, NOT THE TREE (2026-08-06, rf2-owq6p, PR #7616).

WHAT I RULED, one pass earlier: "pin to a commit already on main — the measurement happened upstream of the documenting edit, so no merge can move it." I recorded it as a memory and put it in a brief.

WHY IT IS WRONG AS A GENERAL RULE: it holds for the SSR spike, where the run was taken on an UNMODIFIED MAIN TREE. But MOST of this evidence corpus measures the workers OWN INSTRUMENT CHANGES — so the measured tree was never on main, and NO COMMIT CARRIES IT. The landed commit sits on a LATER BASE. Re-pinning therefore restores the PATCH, not the TREE that was measured.

THE FAILURE IT CAUSES IS WORSE THAN THE DEFECT: an unresolvable pin is VISIBLY broken. A re-pinned wrong one is RESOLVABLE AND WRONG — it fails silently, which is precisely what the bead exists to prevent. Measured: for 9 of 11 pins the rebase preserved every contributed blob and re-pinning was safe; for TWO it did not (one rebase resolved conflicts in three files on the measured path, another moved the file its decomposition turns on) and those were ANNOTATED rather than re-pinned.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, which belongs in the convention rather than in judgement: RE-PIN ONLY WHERE THE REBASE PRESERVED EVERY BLOB THE COMMIT CONTRIBUTED. Otherwise the page says so.

AND THE ENFORCEABLE RULE IS NOT MINE EITHER: not "no authored heads" and not "every SHA must be on main", because several pages deliberately RETAIN the authored head alongside a blob-table fallback and a must-be-on-main gate would red them for being careful. It is "EVERY CITED AUTHORED HEAD MUST BE ACCOMPANIED BY A RESOLVABLE LANDED SHA".

SCALE, so the shape is not mistaken for an edge case: 319 unique hex tokens under docs/design/hicasso/**, of which only 77 are commits — 188 are content digests and FNV hashes that must not be treated as pins at all. 44 stranded, 79 occurrences, 24 pages, ALL reachable from no remote ref.

TWO METHOD NOTES WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX. (1) The recovery was VALIDATED BEFORE BEING TRUSTED, against three pages that already document authored->landed mappings as ground truth: stable patch-id is invariant across this repos rebase-merge, and 43/44 mapped exactly. (2) The worker caught its OWN first blob check comparing WHOLE TREES — which differ for every rebased pair, so it would have condemned everything; the correct check is the commits OWN CONTRIBUTED BLOBS.

THE PATTERN IN MY OWN ERROR, for the seventh time today: I generalised a cure that was correct for ONE case into a rule for a corpus I had not measured. Same shape as generalising the CRLF override from one file to a tree, and the git-grep hazard from one ref to all refs. A CURE THAT WORKED ONCE IS A DATA POINT, NOT A CONVENTION.

A THROW INSIDE A REACT EVENT HANDLER DOES NOT FAIL cljs.test — THE ROW READS GREEN OVER A LIVE EXCEPTION (2026-08-03, rf2-fki5d).

React does not let an exception escape dispatchEvent; it routes it to reportError. So a cljs.test deftest that dispatches a real DOM event and asserts 'nothing threw' sees 0 failures / 0 errors EVEN WHEN THE HANDLER THREW. The rf2-fki5d worker wrote exactly such a row first, and it passed while the code under test was raising InvalidStateError on every run.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: the runner's separate uncaught-pageerror gate (rf2-mwx08) failed the build FROM OUTSIDE the test. So the signal existed, but it was not attached to the assertion that claimed to cover the behaviour — the row itself was fail-open.

THE FIX, and it generalises: any row asserting 'this did not throw' inside a React event must install a window 'error' listener (and assert on it) so the row REDS BY NAME. Otherwise the only coverage of that case is a build-level gate that names no test.

DISPATCH RULE: when briefing browser/DOM work whose claim is 'no exception', require the listener explicitly and require a MUTATION PROOF — delete the fix, confirm the suite exits 1 with exactly one named failure. rf2-fki5d did this and it is what makes the row trustworthy.

RELATED CLASS (same shape, different mask): piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's exit status, not the runner's. Both are fail-open instruments that report success while the thing under test is broken. Distrust any green whose failure path you have not personally mutated.

I DISPATCHED FROM `bd ready` OUTPUT WITHOUT RUNNING `bd show` — AND `bd ready` IS A TITLE LIST (2026-08-06).

WHAT HAPPENED. Dispatching four workers, I ran `bd show` and read bottom-up for three of them and briefed the fourth (rf2-6ckzl) from its line in `bd ready --limit 0`. That line is the TITLE. The title said "cljs_prod / bundle_isolation are not armed by examples/*". THAT WORK HAD LANDED THE PREVIOUS DAY, in c1e833bb4c. The bead was open because its NEWEST NOTE carried a completely different charge - an audit follow-up on PR #7542 about check_gate_scheduling.py reading reachability off raw YAML. The worker verified rather than re-doing, found the arm already present, and did the real work instead.

WHY THIS EVADES THE RULE I ALREADY HAVE. I have a memory that says brief from the newest note, not the title - and I APPLIED IT to the other three beads in the same dispatch pass. The failure was not forgetting the rule; it was that `bd ready` PRESENTS A TITLE and a title is the oldest text on a bead. A bead reopened by an audit keeps its original title forever, so THE READY LIST SYSTEMATICALLY SHOWS THE STALEST DESCRIPTION OF EVERY REOPENED BEAD. On a board where a merged-PR audit reopens roughly one bead per merge, that is most of the reopened pool.

THE MECHANICAL RULE: `bd ready` IS FOR SELECTION, NEVER FOR BRIEFING. Every dispatch needs its own `bd show <id>` read bottom-up, without exception - including the "obvious" small one you are adding to fill a slot. The slot-filler is exactly where the shortcut gets taken.

AND THE INSTRUCTION THAT SAVED IT, again: the brief carried "THE BEAD OUTRANKS THIS BRIEF - read it bottom-up, newest note first, description LAST. Tell me where I am wrong." The worker opened with exactly that correction. That sentence has now caught five wrong briefs of mine. It is a MECHANISM, not a courtesy, and must never be trimmed for brevity.

COROLLARY WORTH KEEPING: also tell the worker WHY the title may be stale (an audit reopen keeps the original title), so it knows to look for the divergence rather than assuming the brief and bead simply disagree.

REAGENT 2.0.1 SWALLOWS :on-recoverable-error — hydration error-capture harnesses built on reagent.dom.client/hydrate-root are VACUOUS. Found by the rf2-53lsj worker (#6407) on 2026-07-19, in its OWN test harness, before shipping. Reagent destructures :on-recoverable-error and NEVER PASSES IT to React hydrateRoot, so the callback fires for nothing: the harness captured NOTHING on either input and passed identically on broken and fixed HTML. Driving React hydrateRoot DIRECTLY, React 19 correctly reports the mismatch ("Hydration failed... + revenue / - :revenue").
RULE: to assert on hydration mismatches, call React hydrateRoot directly. Do not route through Reagent for error capture. And whatever harness you use, PROVE IT CAPTURES: feed it known-bad input and confirm it reports, before trusting a green on good input.
SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME PR, easy to get backwards: Reagent renders a keyword/symbol child via (name x), which DROPS THE NAMESPACE — :a/b renders as "b", not "a/b". A JVM emitter fix that merely strips the leading colon would emit "a/b" and leave the hosts FURTHER apart while appearing closer. Namespaced symbols diverge identically. Always diff the actual BYTES against the client, never reason about the shape.

Reagent's get-react-key (reagent2.impl.template L407) only reads :key meta from VECTORS. ^{:key k} attached to a function-call list form (e.g. ^{:key g} (group-section g …)) is lost on evaluation — the meta lives on the source list at READ time, not on the returned value. Two fixes: (a) put ^{:key k} on the vector literal returned by the function, or (b) wrap the result in (with-meta result {:key k}). Found in views_view.cljs PR #1471 fixing rf2-gphsi; same anti-pattern exists across several other panels (audit bead rf2-?? filed). Tell future test authors: a test that asserts :key meta on the rendered child reproduces the bug.

REAPING ON 'PR MERGED + AGENT REPORTED' STILL CATCHES LIVE AGENTS — twice now, and the guard saved it both times (2026-08-02).

WHAT HAPPENS: an agent sends its final report, the mayor merges its PR and reaps the worktree — and the agent is STILL RUNNING. It keeps working after reporting: extra confirmatory reruns, a last gate, tidying. The worktree vanishes under its cwd and its background process dies.

INCIDENTS: the heap worker (reaped on PR-merge while alive; recorded then as 'reap only when merged AND reported'), and now proc-6tags-7uxkt — which HAD reported done, then set up a node_modules junction and started an extra test:cljs run. It found its worktree gone mid-run.

WHY IT HAS BEEN HARMLESS BOTH TIMES, and this is the load-bearing part: scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh disarms the node_modules junction BEFORE removing, so the junction-following hazard (which has emptied the mayor's real node_modules twice historically) did NOT fire. Canary held at 101 entries across both incidents. The worker's commits were pushed before reporting, so nothing was lost either time.

THE REFINEMENT, since 'reported done' is evidently not the same as 'finished': the cheap check before reaping a just-merged worktree is whether its agent is still live (a task notification arriving after the report is the tell; so is a recent mtime under the worktree). It costs one look. But the honest weighting is that the GUARD is the real protection and it works — this is a courtesy to the worker's last few minutes, not a safety issue. Do not build ceremony around it; do not skip the guard.

DO NOT force removal or bypass the guard when a reap refuses — a refusal means something still holds the tree, which is exactly when following a junction would be catastrophic.

MY INLINE REAP DELETED A WORKTREE WHILE ITS WORKER WAS STILL GATING, AND THE GATE FAILED FALSELY (2026-08-04).

WHAT HAPPENED. Earlier in the session I twice merged a PR and forgot to reap its worktree, so I folded the reap INTO the merge loop to make it unskippable. That fixed the leak and introduced a worse failure: a worker was still running the fast-PR spine in the worktree I deleted. PR #7469 merged at 02:24:42 UTC; the branch and worktree were removed; the worker's spine finished at 02:24:53, eleven seconds later, reading a directory that no longer existed. It reported FAIL implementation JS harness helpers with 11 reagent-slim policy failures, all of the form "Cannot find module", "missing workflow: .github/workflows/test.yml", "missing changed-surfaces script" -- files that are tracked in git and were present. The worker correctly discarded the result under the killed-gate rule and confirmed the CI counterpart was SUCCESS on main.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS BEYOND THE WASTED RUN. The failure LOOKS like a real policy regression naming real files. A worker with less discipline would have "fixed" the missing modules, or reported a red that does not exist. It is the mirror of the backgrounded-gate bug we fixed today, where a relative invocation graded ANOTHER worktree: same class, opposite direction -- the gate reads a tree that is not the one it thinks it is reading.

THE RULE: A MERGE DOES NOT MEAN THE WORKER HAS EXITED. The PR opening is the worker's LAST reported act, not its last act -- it may still be running gates, updating the PR body, or answering a message. Before reaping a worktree, confirm the worker is actually done: no live agent for that bead, or the worktree quiescent across a tick. When in doubt, leave the worktree; a stale directory costs disk, a deleted one costs a false red and possibly a spurious "fix".

THE CORRECTED SHAPE: keep the reap adjacent to the merge so it cannot be forgotten, but gate it on the worker being finished rather than on the PR being merged. Reaping on the NEXT tick after the merge is the cheap approximation and is what I should do by default.

RELATED, SAME SESSION: the same worker corrected two claims of mine. Local clj-kondo here is 2025.10.23 while CI pins 2026.04.15; the local build reports 0 errors on the line CI fails and 10 different errors CI does not, so a local clj-kondo pass proves nothing about the gate -- fetch the pinned binary. And my "the tree has exactly one suppression" figure was ESLINT's census applied to CLJ-KONDO: there are at least four #_:clj-kondo/ignore sites. A census of one linter says nothing about another.

REAP A WORKER WORKTREE ONLY WHEN ITS AGENT REPORTS DONE — NOT WHEN ITS PR MERGES (2026-08-01, my error).

WHAT I DID: after merging PR #7337 I ran scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh against worker/heapaxis-2rtt6-34. The removal FAILED on a Windows file lock, but the guard had already done its first job and DISARMED THE node_modules JUNCTION. The agent was still alive. Its next shadow-cljs call failed with 'shadow-cljs not found' and it spent a tool round diagnosing before reporting 'my worktree junction has vanished... Recreating it'. It self-recovered and the mayor's real node_modules stayed intact at 101, so no damage — but I cost a live worker a pointless detour.

THE MISTAKE IS THE TRIGGER, NOT THE SCRIPT. A merged PR means the WORK landed; it does NOT mean the AGENT finished. Agents legitimately keep working after opening a PR: updating the PR body, re-running a gate, hardening a mutation proof, answering a resume message.

THE RULE: reap only when BOTH hold — (1) the PR is merged, AND (2) the agent has reported done or is confirmed dead. A reap that fails on a file lock is often a SIGNAL the tree is still in use: check whether the agent is alive before retrying, and never retry in a loop.

STILL TRUE AND UNCHANGED: the guard is right to unlink the junction BEFORE removing (that is what stops git worktree remove following it into the mayor's real node_modules), and right to refuse rather than force when removal cannot complete. The defect was entirely in WHEN I invoked it.

REBASE conflict resolution: --ours/--theirs INVERT vs merge. In a rebase, --ours = the branch you are replaying ONTO (e.g. origin/main), --theirs = the commit being replayed (the worker's own branch). So to take MAIN's version of a generated file (e.g. docs/cljs/playground-rf2.js) during a rebase, use 'git checkout --ours <file>', NOT --theirs. My earlier dispatch instructions said --theirs for this and were WRONG (caught by the rf2-ywwpx worker on #6284, 2026-07-18, which verified empirically: stage2/--ours == origin/main, stage3/--theirs == its own stale commit). Harmless for a generated file that gets regenerated afterwards, but on a NON-generated conflict the same wording silently takes the wrong side and can revert main's work. ALWAYS instruct workers to verify which stage matches origin/main (git show :2:<file> / :3:<file> and compare digests) rather than trusting the label.

Rebase-merge makes a worker branch look UNMERGED to an ancestry check. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` returns N>0 and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` fails for a branch whose PR was merged with --rebase, because the rebase rewrote the SHAs. Judging 'abandoned, holds unmerged work' from that heuristic mislabelled 7 of 9 branches in one hygiene pass (their PRs #7096-#7107 were all merged). The authoritative test is PATCH-ID containment: `git cherry origin/main origin/<branch>` counting '^+' lines == 0 means fully merged. Confirm with `gh pr view --json state` == MERGED as the second signal.

A MERGE TIMESTAMP EARLIER THAN A RUN'S START DOES NOT MEAN THE RUN'S TREE CONTAINED THAT CHANGE — this repo rebase-merges (found 2026-08-07, rf2-jv36i).

WHAT HAPPENED. A bead assumed 'the codec change is on main by then' because PR #7390 merged at 18:06:11Z and the measurement windows ran 18:14:02Z-18:21:10Z. Eight minutes clear, in wall clock. But the run was taken from a worker branch based at b4144427ec, authored BEFORE the change landed and rebase-merged AFTER. The landed history orders the commits correctly; the measured tree never contained them.

WHY IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG. Under rebase-merge the branch tip that produced a measurement is not an ancestor of main at all, and its base can predate several landings that appear, in main's log, to sit before the run. Reading merge times off main and comparing them to a run's clock is exactly the wrong instrument.

HOW TO CHECK PROPERLY — any one of these settles it, and they should agree:
  - BLOB: the evidence page stamps the blob of the file under test; compare it to the change's before/after blobs. This is the strongest check because it names what was actually loaded.
  - ANCESTRY: 'git merge-base --is-ancestor <change-commit> <producing-commit>' — NO means the tree lacked it.
  - BASE: what commit the producing branch was cut from, and what that tree's relevant blob was.

RELATED, same root cause: a stranded authored head's patch-id may differ from its landed counterpart because the rebase resolved conflicts — so 'the patch landed' and 'this tree was measured' are separate questions, and provenance prose must not conflate them.

A PROVENANCE PIN NAMING AN AUTHORED SHA IS STRANDED BY REBASE-MERGE — THE PAGE LOOKS PINNED AND IS NOT (2026-08-06, rf2-zn7pj / PR #7610; scope filed as rf2-owq6p).

THE FINDING: the SSR spike witness pinned its evidence to 952a3f2024. That commit IS NOT AN ANCESTOR OF MAIN, and neither is its sibling 6f40304011. This repo REBASE-MERGES, which rewrites SHAs, so the authored head a page names is stranded the moment its PR merges. Verified with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` returning non-zero.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE STALE FIGURES IT WAS FILED FOR: stale figures under a RESOLVABLE pin are checkable and wrong, which is a normal defect. Figures under an UNRESOLVABLE pin are NOT CHECKABLE AT ALL — a reader cannot obtain the tree the measurement was taken on. The pages central verifiability claim fails SILENTLY, and it fails while looking rigorous. This is the evidence-corpus form of the fail-open class.

THE FIX THAT DISSOLVES IT: PIN TO A COMMIT ALREADY ON MAIN. The measurement happens upstream of the documenting edit, so no merge of the documenting PR can move it — main advanced eight commits during that pass and the pin never had to change. Do not pin to your own branch head.

AND THE REASONING THAT DECLINED A BLOB TABLE, which is the better half: a blob table pins the INSTRUMENT when the anchor cannot be pinned. Here the anchor CAN be pinned, and a resolvable whole-tree SHA pins strictly more. It would also PIN LESS THAN IT LOOKS — the clock pages magnitudes are a function of three driver files, whereas these figures are a SHA-256 over a whole document plus a boundary census, a function of corpus, entry, substrate, adapter and the pinned react-dom. A short blob table would ADVERTISE A CLOSURE IT DOES NOT HAVE. Ask what the artefact is actually a function of before choosing what to pin.

RELATED, ALREADY KNOWN: `git merge-base --is-ancestor` and `git cherry` disagree for the same reason — rebase-merge rewrites SHAs, so ancestry says "unmerged" for branches that are fully merged. Same mechanism, two different wrong conclusions: there it under-reports merge status, here it strands a citation.

TWO NON-MANUFACTURES FROM THE SAME PASS WORTH COPYING. (1) X1(b)s +16 bytes was LEFT UNDECOMPOSED: the ruler moved AND the document drifted, and only X1(a) can separate its share because rf2-2rtt6.114 measured independently — no second instrument exists for the canonical DOM. The worker checked whether em dashes explained it, found the dogfood titles are ASCII, and STATED THE SUM rather than guessing. (2) The X3 refusal control turned out NOT DETERMINISTIC under load — one take refused at phase 2, another qualified throughout. It published what it got, said the 0.3 ms knob sits inside the boxs noise, and noted the 2 ms production ceiling is far from that regime, rather than re-running until the expected shape returned. Re-running until a control behaves is how a control stops being one.

AND A GATE BLIND SPOT IT CAUGHT ON ITSELF: an edit DROPPED A `## X1(b)` HEADING and `check_doc_slugs.py` passed it, because nothing links to that anchor. A heading with no inbound link can vanish silently. Diff headings against HEAD when editing a structured evidence page.

A GATE CONFLATED "THE TEST FAILED" WITH "THE TEST NEVER RAN", AND THE DISCRIMINATOR IS WHETHER THE RUNNER PRINTED ITS OWN COUNT (2026-08-06, rf2-v8561, PR #7608).

THE REPORTED DEFECT: three CLJS namespaces failing per-namespace isolation. It did NOT reproduce — clean worktree, fresh npm ci, fresh compile, the beads own repro command twice, exit 0 both times, and all 17 roster namespaces green alone (196 tests / 731 assertions).

THE TELL THAT CRACKED IT, and it is the kind of thing only a fresh reading finds: THE THREE REPORTED NAMESPACES ARE THE LAST THREE ROSTER ENTRIES, CONSECUTIVELY. That is not three independent fixture defects — it is a CONTIGUOUS TAIL, the signature of something collapsing partway through a sweep that spawns one node process per namespace over 276 measured seconds.

THE CAUSE: compile-node-test.cjs UNLINKS out/node-test.js before every compile, deliberately, so a failed compile leaves nothing stale (rf2-6t03c). A compile starting mid-sweep pulls the bundle out from under every run still to come. Injecting exactly that at t=225s of a 276s sweep reds EXACTLY THOSE THREE NAMESPACES, namespace for namespace. Both recorded sightings were worktrees with other builds running.

THE STRUCTURAL DISCRIMINATOR, which is the reusable part: --test=<ns> is a RUNTIME selector over a bundle that links EVERY test namespace, so A MODULE-LOAD CRASH CANNOT SINGLE A NAMESPACE OUT. Therefore: A RED CARRYING "Ran N tests containing M assertions." IS A VERDICT ABOUT THAT NAMESPACE; A RED WITHOUT ONE NEVER WAS. Three causes reach a non-zero standalone exit and the gate was reporting all three as the first — ISOLATION (real leak, fixture remedy), ROSTER (stale curated list; 9dd9633d0b and d3969eb67b are both commits fixing that AFTER the gate blamed fixtures), ENVIRONMENT (bundle vanished; the sweep is INDETERMINATE, exit 2, and ITS GREENS ARE WORTH NO MORE THAN ITS REDS).

TWO RULES TO CARRY:
1. When a gate accuses several namespaces at once, CHECK WHETHER THEY ARE CONTIGUOUS IN ITS ROSTER. Adjacency is evidence of one external event, not of N independent defects. The old gate under an unlink at t=6s accused SIXTEEN namespaces of leaking, every one MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
2. A GREEN MUST ALSO CARRY A NON-ZERO TEST COUNT. This is the same floor as the long-standing "Ran 0 tests reads as green" family, arriving from the opposite direction: there the count was zero because nothing was selected, here because nothing could load.

SIBLING TO CHECK, filed as rf2-1wyyb: check-ui-adapter-isolation.cjs has the same --self-test shape and plausibly the same conflation. Not verified — a shared filename pattern is not evidence of a shared defect.

Redaction/privacy threat model for re-frame2 dev tools (Story/Xray/MCP/share): a local programmer can ALWAYS reach secrets programmatically (eval, direct app-db), so redacting sensitive values from the human USING the tool is futile and NOT the goal. Only two concerns: (1) maybe handing them to an AI/LLM (MCP/agent payloads) — a soft 'maybe', and largely already handled by the MCP servers' --allow-sensitive-reads gate (OFF by default, forces :rf/redacted elision); (2) firmer: stopping them being written to logs. Implication: human-facing egress (share URLs, static export, copied EDN, screenshots of the dev's own app) is NOT privacy-blocked — unblock it. Scope rf2-qarwq narrowly to the AI boundary + logs; do not gold-plate. StoryUI packet's 'BLOCKED until common egress seam' framing (02 sec15, 04, story S11) is over-cautious against this model. -- Mike, 2026-05-30

REFINEMENT OF MY OWN FINDING FROM EARLIER TODAY — WELL-EVIDENCED CLOSES ALSO GET REOPENED, AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT PHENOMENON (2026-07-26).

EARLIER I MEASURED that gate/fixture beads closed on ARMING rather than on CATCHING are the largest category the merged-PR audit reopens, and concluded that a meaningful share of the reopen rate is my own close quality. That is true and the remediation stands.

BUT IT IS INCOMPLETE. Checking again a few hours later: FIVE beads I closed TODAY WITH FULL MUTATION EVIDENCE are open again — rf2-5o52l, rf2-12g5z, rf2-4hc9p, rf2-isp3i, rf2-lnecd — and every one carries NEW-RESIDUAL language rather than a restatement of the original defect. rf2-5o52l is the clearest: the emit-site privacy direction was accepted as correct, and the reopen names a DIFFERENT thing the SSR widening changed in the hydrate and restore :skews accumulators.

SO THERE ARE TWO DISTINCT REOPEN CLASSES AND THEY NEED DIFFERENT RESPONSES:
  (A) WEAK-CLOSE REOPENS — the close said the job was added / the roster widened / the suite is green, giving the audit nothing to verify against. The audit then does the verification I should have done. FIX: mutation proof in the close reason. Mine to prevent.
  (B) NEW-RESIDUAL REOPENS — the close was fully evidenced and ACCEPTED, and the audit found something ELSE by examining the merged code. This is the audit working as designed and is NOT a defect in my closing. Treating it as one would push me toward defensive over-closing, which is worse.

HOW TO TELL THEM APART IN ONE READ: does the reopen note ENGAGE WITH the close evidence and then name something new ("the emit-site direction is correct, BUT the SSR widening changed..."), or does it re-assert the original defect? The former is (B) and is fresh work. The latter is (A) and is my failure.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE BACKLOG NUMBER: I have been treating roughly one reopen per merged PR as partly my fault. Half of it is; the other half is the audit finding genuinely new defects in freshly merged code, which is exactly what it is for and which no improvement in my close reasons will reduce. So the open count will NOT converge to zero while the audit runs, and that is a property of the system rather than a throughput failure. Report it that way.

THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is one I keep relearning: a measured finding is usually true of the subset I measured, not of the whole. My first pass looked only at gate beads and generalised. Checking a wider sample a few hours later split the finding in two. BEFORE ACTING ON A MEASURED PATTERN, ASK WHICH POPULATION IT WAS MEASURED OVER.
Refinements added to an IN_PROGRESS bead rarely reach the worker (they have already read the spec and are coding). File a NEW follow-up bead instead of noting the in-progress one. (Mike, 2026-05-31)

WHEN A WORKER REPORTS FIXING SOMETHING IN PASSING, CHECK WHETHER A LIVE WORKER OWNS THE SAME CODE — AND RELAY IT. Cost duplicate work on 2026-07-24.

WHAT HAPPENED: the F5h virtual-table pilot hit a cross-mode bug while building its pilot — node/classify-event asked fn? and a roster callback is a RECORD, so an interpreted [:div {:on-scroll (v/event ...)}] was unrenderable on the structural host. It fixed that in passing (one spec-cited clause) and reported it as its finding 1. SEPARATELY, the emitter silent-drop worker was mid-flight on rf2-berc2, whose fix REQUIRES the same function to stop refusing a Callback — so it fixed it too, independently, with a different marker.

I HAD THE PILOT REPORT IN HAND AND DID NOT RELAY IT. The overlap only surfaced at rebase time as a conflict in node.cljc and in the pilot_overlay witness test.

⚠️ THE OUTCOME WAS ACTUALLY GOOD, and the reason is worth keeping: main version had RULED THE QUESTION DIFFERENTLY — it records the mode-neutral {:rf.ui/opaque :fn} member, with a docstring citing 004B as the authority, where the second worker had a per-role marker (:v/event / :v/handler). Two independent attempts surfaced a design choice neither brief had posed. The second worker resolved correctly: took main version explicitly with `git checkout origin/main -- <file>` rather than an --ours/--theirs label, then PROVED nothing was lost (`git diff origin/main -- <files>` empty, plus `git show <old-sha> -- <files>` confirming its contribution was the same repair and therefore subsumed), and fixed two of its own test docstrings that still described the superseded marker.

THE MAYOR RULE: when a worker report says "I also fixed X" or "I had to repair Y to proceed", immediately check the in-flight set for anyone whose bead touches X or Y, and SEND THEM A MESSAGE. It costs one tool call. The alternative is a rebase conflict discovered late, in a file where one side may carry a WITNESS TEST the other side flipped differently — and witness collisions are how the trunk goes red.

RELATED, ALREADY RECORDED: two workers must never share a surface. This is the softer version — a worker that fixes something OUTSIDE its stated surface silently creates a shared surface nobody declared. Incidental fixes are legitimate and often necessary; the coordination burden falls on the mayor, not on them.

REOPEN-NOTE DISCRIMINATOR GREP WAS TOO NARROW — I RE-CLOSED OVER A LIVE AUDIT FINDING (2026-07-25). To tell my own checkout-race reverts apart from genuine reviewer reopens I grepped bead notes for "AUDIT-REOPEN|MERGED-PR AUDIT". rf2-zt65l carried a note spelled "AUDIT REOPEN (PR #6921 ...)" — SPACE, not hyphen — so my grep returned 0, I concluded "my race, not a reviewer", and re-closed a bead whose audit finding was still unmet. The audit then reopened it with an explicit correction: "a concurrent checkpoint re-closed this owner while claiming it contained zero audit-reopen notes." That is exactly the failure mode I had been guarding against all session, produced by my own detection code. CORRECTED PATTERN, use this: grep -ciE "audit.?reopen|merged-pr audit|reopened|REOPEN" — case-insensitive, tolerant of hyphen/space/underscore, and including bare "REOPENED" which several audits use as the leading verb. BETTER STILL: do not rely on a single grep. Before re-closing ANY bead that reads open after you closed it, READ the recent notes (bd show | tail) with your eyes. A close is destructive to an audit obligation and cheap to defer; when the two hypotheses are "my tooling reverted it" and "a reviewer reopened it with a finding", the cost of being wrong is asymmetric — assume reviewer unless the notes plainly show otherwise. THE UNDERLYING LESSON, which recurs: a negative grep result is weak evidence. It proves your PATTERN did not match, never that the THING is absent. Same class as "grep -c beads <file> || echo NO HOOK" (grep exits 1 on zero count, not only on a missing file) and the "&& / ||" precedence bug that truncated issues.jsonl. Three instances this session, one root cause: treating shell/grep exit semantics as a truth oracle.

A REPO-WIDE GREP MATCHES .beads/issues.jsonl — SO IT FINDS DISCUSSION *ABOUT* CODE AND COUNTS IT AS CODE. Cost me a wrong inference on 2026-07-24.

WHAT HAPPENED: I grepped for a carrier slot in rules/rejected-prop-spellings and got 3 hits, and concluded the forgery guard had shipped. The rf2-drpa3.132 worker reproduced it properly and found the roster on main has 6 entries and CONTAINS NO CALLER SLOT. My "3 hits" were .beads/issues.jsonl noise (the export contains every bead prose, including my own notes describing the thing I was looking for) plus one unrelated node.cljc match. The forgery guard was NOT delivered — reproduced as 27 failures and 2 errors against unmodified main.

⚠️ THE SELF-REFERENTIAL TRAP IS THE NASTY PART: I had WRITTEN a bead note saying "the caller carrier appears in rules/rejected-prop-spellings", that note went into the export, and my later grep found my own note and treated it as evidence for the claim. The tracker export turns a search for evidence into a search that can find its own hypothesis.

THE RULE: when grepping to establish whether code exists, EXCLUDE the tracker export and other generated/derived files:
  git grep <pattern> -- implementation/ spec/ docs/     # scope it
  or at minimum:  grep -r ... --exclude-dir=.beads
And prefer `git grep` over `grep -r`: it searches TRACKED files and respects pathspecs, which makes scoping natural.

THE statusCheckRollup LAGS THE BRANCH IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — THE BRANCH QUERY IS GROUND TRUTH (observed twice, 2026-08-07).

DIRECTION 1, too OPTIMISTIC: the rollup reported ok=78 canc=0 fail=0 pend=0 total=78 — settled by every field it exposes — while "gh run list --branch" showed TWO runs QUEUED. A queued run has no checks attached to the head commit yet, so the rollup does not know they are coming. Merging there ships a PR two workflows short.

DIRECTION 2, too PESSIMISTIC: the rollup reported two checks IN_PROGRESS ("CLJS (shadow-cljs :node-test)" and "JVM tools/template") while "gh run list --branch" showed ALL FIVE workflows completed/success at that exact head sha. Here the rollup holds stale entries from a superseded run; the work is done and the PR is genuinely green.

SO: clause 3 (zero QUEUED/IN_PROGRESS in the rollup) is NOT sufficient and NOT necessary on its own. The authoritative question is always the branch, keyed to the CURRENT head sha:
  gh run list --branch <headRefName> --limit 25 --json workflowName,status,conclusion,headSha
and then: every workflow at that sha is completed with conclusion success (or a deliberate skip), and none is queued or in_progress.

WHEN THEY DISAGREE, BELIEVE THE BRANCH — but say in the report that they disagreed and which way, because a reader checking later will see only one of them. Do not merge on a rollup that is more optimistic than the branch; do not block forever on a rollup that is more pessimistic than it.

This is the same lesson as everything else in this family: a summary that is derived, cached or lagged is not the fact. Go to the thing that ran.

statusCheckRollup CAN REPORT ZERO PENDING WHILE WORKFLOW RUNS ARE STILL QUEUED (observed 2026-08-07, PR #7630).

WHAT HAPPENED: 'gh pr list --json statusCheckRollup' reported ok=78, cancelled=0, failed=0, PENDING=0, total=78 — a fully concluded rollup by every field it exposes. A queued run's checks are not yet attached to the head commit's rollup, so the rollup does not know they are coming and reports the PR as settled.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS: it is indistinguishable from genuinely complete. The total even LOOKS plausible — 78 against an expected band of ~82-86 — because a re-run had replaced earlier entries and shrunk the count. Merging there ships a PR two workflows short, which is exactly how PR #7628 reached main unverified.

THIS IS THE THIRD DISGUISE OF ONE DEFECT IN A SINGLE SESSION. (1) An EMPTY rollup satisfies '0 fail and 0 pending'. (2) Counting status==COMPLETED as passed silently counts CANCELLED as green. (3) pending==0 while runs are queued. All three report the absence of bad news as the presence of good news.

THE MERGE CRITERION, all four clauses, none sufficient alone:
  - total is non-empty and in the band the repo actually produces (~86 here; verify with 'gh pr checks' on recent merged PRs, do not assume)
  - every conclusion is SUCCESS or SKIPPED — CANCELLED is NOT passed
  - zero QUEUED or IN_PROGRESS entries in the rollup
  - AND 'gh run list --branch <head>' shows no run with status queued or in_progress
The last clause is the one that catches this case, and it needs a second API call. Make it; a merge is not the place to save a round trip.

Every scratchpad artefact gets a name unique to the worker — include the bead id or the branch name (pr-body-rf2-jr0tg.md, not pr-body.md). Prefer WORKTREE-LOCAL paths over the scratchpad entirely for anything a gate or a PR depends on; the worktree genuinely is per-worker. And before believing any file the worker did not just write in that same tool call, confirm it is its own.

THE MAYOR'S SIDE: when concurrent workers are in flight, do not assume a PR body belongs to its PR. Spot-check that the body describes the bead the PR claims, especially when two workers reported close together.

SENDMESSAGE'S OWN RESPONSE IS A RELIABLE WORKER-LIVENESS SIGNAL (discovered 2026-07-25, after four incidents that a reliable signal would have prevented).

The two response shapes mean different things:
  * 'Message queued for delivery to <id> at its next tool round.' => the agent is ALIVE and mid-task. Do not prune its worktree, do not assume its beads are discharged.
  * 'Agent "<id>" had no active task; resumed from transcript in the background with your message.' => the agent was IDLE/COMPLETE at that moment. Its worktree was prunable, and whatever it had was final.

WHY THIS MATTERS: terminality was the fact I kept lacking. I pruned three worktrees from under live workers by inferring done-ness from 'PR merged' plus a clean tree, and I merged two PRs mid-push for the same reason — the merge sweep has PR state in hand while liveness lives in task notifications that arrive asynchronously and repeat (a background agent notifies every time it stops with no live children, so one job notifies several times and 'completed' does NOT mean finished). Freshness helps but is a stale sample: a worker 45 minutes quiet turned out to be mid-write and committed 3 seconds after I looked.

HOW TO USE IT: when terminality is ambiguous and the decision is destructive or finalising (prune, close a bead, treat a merge as complete), send the worker a short status question and READ THE TOOL'S OWN RESPONSE. That is cheap, non-destructive, and definitive at the moment you ask. It also does something useful either way: an alive worker gets your update, an idle one gets resumed with it.

Note the resume side effect: messaging an idle agent RESTARTS it from its transcript. That is usually desirable (it picks up remaining work with fresh context on what changed), but it means the check is not free — do not poll with it, and do not use it on an agent whose work you want left finished.

SEVENTH FALSE-GREEN VECTOR: STALE SHADOW-CLJS CACHE ON AN .EDN-ONLY EDIT (2026-07-25, found by the EP-0037 routing worker). conformance-fixtures INLINES the EDN at compile time and declares no cache dependency on the .edn file — so editing ONLY a fixture .edn does not invalidate the shadow-cljs cache, and the suite recompiles from cache and reports the OLD fixture's verdict. The worker's failing CLJS conformance fixture was this, not a real failure. CI never sees it because CI compiles fresh from a cold cache; it bites LOCAL runs only, which is the worst shape — a worker debugging a red it cannot explain, or worse, a worker whose fixture fix appears not to work and who then 'fixes' something that was never broken.

WORKAROUND: after an .edn-only fixture edit, clear .shadow-cljs (or touch a .cljs/.cljc file in the same build) before believing a local CLJS result. Related known trap: a stale shadow-cljs SERVER JVM after a source-dir rename produces 'namespace not available' — check .shadow-cljs/server.pid age and kill the java pid.

THE FULL LIST OF WAYS A GREEN LIES IN THIS REPO, now seven: (1) piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's status; (2) a compound or backgrounded command's trailing echo supplies a 0 while the log says FAIL — this worker hit it TWICE in one session and caught both by rc capture; (3) test-fast-pr.sh soft-skips its own mkdocs step when mkdocs is off PATH and still exits 0; (4) a .cljc test namespace missing its lane suffix is silently skipped by one runner; (5) a wrapper-reported 'exit code 0' disagreeing with a captured rc; (6) the BACKGROUNDING HARNESS reporting exit code 0 for a run whose log says rc=1; (7) this one — a stale compile cache serving an old inlined fixture.

Note that (7) is different in kind from (1)-(6): those are about MISREADING a verdict, this is about the verdict being computed from stale INPUT. So 'capture rc and cross-check the log' does not catch it. The brief line that does: 'an .edn/data-only edit may not invalidate the CLJS cache — clear .shadow-cljs before trusting a local CLJS result on a data-only change.'

When a worker edits a test namespace then runs node tests, shadow-cljs incremental compile can show a PHANTOM failure referencing the PRE-EDIT test source (a compile race). Fix: force a clean 'npx shadow-cljs compile node-test' before trusting 'node out/node-test.js'. Seen by rf2-2lb7z worker (PR #1946) — first two runs showed a stale 1-failure, clean recompile gave 0. Tell test-authoring workers to recompile-then-run after editing a test ns.

BOTH /tmp AND THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD ARE SHARED ACROSS CONCURRENT AGENTS ON THIS HOST. Two independent workers hit this on 2026-07-24, in two different directories.

INSTANCE 1 — /tmp: a worker gate log written to /tmp/gate-browser.log was overwritten by ANOTHER worker run. It read EXIT=0 and "0 failures" — plausible numbers, wrong code. The only tell was the shadow-cljs "config:" banner naming a different worktree. This defeats the capture-and-echo-the-exit-code discipline, because the captured EXIT CODE belongs to the other run too.

INSTANCE 2 — THE SCRATCHPAD: the v/->react worker had its pr-body.md OVERWRITTEN by another worker mid-task. Caught before it did damage, but a PR body is exactly the kind of file you write once and read back later without re-checking.

THE RULE, now standard in every brief: write worker-owned files to a WORKTREE-LOCAL path, not /tmp and not a bare name in the shared scratchpad. If the scratchpad must be used, make the filename UNIQUE (include the branch or bead id). And VERIFY OWNERSHIP before believing any captured artefact — for a shadow-cljs run, the "config:" banner names the worktree whose build ran; grep it and confirm it is yours.

GENERAL FORM, which is why this outlives both instances: when an assertion or an artefact rests on something OUTSIDE your process — a shared temp directory, a shared port, a shared cache, a scratchpad — ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read back. A file you wrote is not necessarily the file you read. This is the same family as the console-shim trap (the observer sits below your runtime) and the attribute-order trap (the serialisation carries incidental detail) — in every case the thing being measured is not the thing you think you are measuring.

MAYOR NOTE: my own boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log" for a long stretch of dispatches. Saturating six workers on one machine makes shared-path collision the NORMAL case, not an edge case.

SHARED SCRATCHPAD CAN OVERWRITE A LIVE WORKER'S FILE MID-TASK (2026-07-25, second occurrence, escalating). Concurrent workers share one temp root. First occurrence: a worker reached for scratchpad/pr-body.md and found ANOTHER worker's PR body already in it — caught by a stale-read refusal. Second occurrence: the R6 worker's own scratchpad file was ACTIVELY OVERWRITTEN mid-task by a different PR's body content, and it only noticed because a python string-replace threw on a missing substring. Its own assessment: 'a silent overwrite of a body file could have published the wrong description' — i.e. gh pr edit --body-file could publish another PR's text under your PR.

AGENT-QUALIFIED FILENAMES ARE NOT SUFFICIENT — the second victim was already using them. Brief workers to: (1) write PR bodies inside their OWN WORKTREE (a gitignored path like <worktree>/ai/gate-logs/ or <worktree>/.worker/), never the shared session scratchpad; (2) verify content immediately before publishing — re-read the file and confirm it contains an expected marker unique to THIS PR; (3) treat a string-replace that fails to find its substring as a CORRUPTION SIGNAL, not a bug in the pattern. The R6 worker's recovery is the right pattern: it treated the live PR body on GitHub as the source of truth and rebuilt from that rather than trusting local state.

Related mayor-side trap from the same session: Git Bash /tmp and Windows Python /tmp are DIFFERENT paths. Python raised FileNotFoundError while a following 'gh pr edit --body-file /tmp/...' happily re-uploaded the UNMODIFIED file — a chain that reported success while doing nothing. Gate any publish on the editing step's own return code.

A GATE THAT IS SILENT ON SUCCESS GIVES AN EXIT 0 THAT CANNOT BE DISTINGUISHED FROM IT SKIPPING YOUR FILE (observed 2026-08-07, PR #7638).

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker ran 'python scripts/check_provenance_pins.py --changed-since origin/main' and got exit 0 with NO OUTPUT AT ALL. That is exactly what the gate prints when it selects your page and finds nothing wrong — and also exactly what it would print if it selected NO pages, or skipped yours. The worker re-ran with --verbose specifically so the claim 'it stayed green on that page' was evidence rather than inference. The verbose run showed '1 files, 5 cited pins' — proving the page was actually examined.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE GATE ITSELF POLICES: a fail-open is a check that passes without checking. A silent exit 0 lets a worker report 'the gate is green on my change' when the gate may never have looked at it. check_doc_slugs.py has the same property — silent on success.

THE RULE: for any gate that is silent on success, run it with --verbose (or its equivalent) and QUOTE THE LINE SHOWING IT SELECTED YOUR FILES. 'exit 0' alone is not evidence the gate covered the surface; it is only evidence the gate did not fail. This is the same reasoning as never nominating a gate whose exclusion list omits the tree being edited — mkdocs --strict exits 0 over docs/design/** having verified nothing.

FOR THE MAYOR: when a worker reports a silent gate at exit 0 with no selection evidence, ask which files it selected before treating the surface as covered.

SIXTH FALSE-GREEN VECTOR, and this one is THE HARNESS ITSELF (2026-07-25). A worker's backgrounded gate reported success while the gate had failed: sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh was backgrounded on timeout, and the task-completion NOTIFICATION said 'exit code 0' while the script itself had printed rc=1 in its log. The worker caught it only by READING THE LOG rather than believing the notification.

So the list of ways a green can lie in this repo is now: (1) piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's status; (2) a compound or backgrounded command's trailing echo supplies a 0 while the log says FAIL; (3) test-fast-pr.sh soft-skips its own mkdocs step when mkdocs is off PATH and still exits 0; (4) a .cljc test namespace missing its lane suffix is silently skipped by one runner; (5) a wrapper-reported 'exit code 0' disagreeing with a captured rc (the v/custom-element slice hit this, and the captured 1 was correct — it is what surfaced a live defect); and now (6) the BACKGROUNDING HARNESS reporting exit code 0 for a run whose log says rc=1.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE WORKER: (6) breaks the mitigation for (1)-(3). 'Capture rc immediately and never pipe' is defeated if the layer REPORTING the rc is itself wrong. So the brief line must be stronger than 'capture the exit code': it must be 'cross-check the captured rc against the log's own PASS/FAIL lines, and treat any disagreement as failure until proven otherwise.' I have been writing that in briefs; this is the incident that justifies it, so keep it.

THE UNDERLYING FAILURE was environmental and worth knowing on its own: a FRESH WORKTREE HAS NO implementation/node_modules, so shadow-cljs is not on PATH and the 'CLJS node integration' step dies. Everything before that step was genuinely green. Fix is npm ci inside the worker's OWN worktree — never a junction into the mayor tree, which once deleted the mayor's real node_modules.

Worker gotcha (2026-06-10, bit hiqtk8 #3700): the CI gate 'Verify skill ↔ MCP allowed-tools drift' is a MULTI-script job; one axis is check_skill_implementor_partition_drift.py rule L7 (BEAD-ID-LEAK) = user-facing skill leaves (SKILL.md / README.md / references/*.md under skills/) must carry ZERO 'rf2-' bead ids. A worker that adds an explanatory parenthetical like '(... removed per rf2-XXXXX)' into a skill doc FAILS this gate. FIX: strip the tracker-id, keep the substantive sentence. BRIEF RULE: any worker editing skills/ must NOT cite rf2- bead ids in skill prose.

THE SPINE SKIPS EVERYTHING WHEN THERE IS NO DIFF, so a POST-MERGE verification run proves nothing unless you pass --all (2026-08-05).

THE MECHANISM: scripts/test-fast-pr.sh classifies surfaces from the diff against origin/main. In a checkout whose commits are ALREADY MERGED, there is no diff, so it self-classifies docs=false jvm=false node=false and exits 0 having run nothing of consequence. The rf2-l0wfx worker hit this while re-verifying after I merged its PR out from under it: the plain spine went green while skipping the docs lane its EP-0038 edit needed. It re-ran with --all and got a real result.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE WORKER: I have twice merged a PR while its worker was still verifying. The natural recovery - "re-run the gates against merged main" - is exactly the case where the plain spine is vacuous. So the recovery from my mistake has its own fail-open, and a worker following it would report PASS having tested nothing.

THE RULE: any verification run in a checkout with no diff against origin/main MUST use --all. If a report says "re-ran the spine against merged main, exit 0", ask whether it was --all; a bare pass there is the same shape as the tools/template lane skipped on main, and as check_doc_slugs.py exiting 0 over TESTING.md which it never opens.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING, from the same run: the --all log contains a FAIL token that is a self-test DESCRIPTION string - "a single standalone failure is flagged as the red namespace (FAIL path)". Grepping the log for FAIL finds it. Read the runner's own terminal marker, not a grep.

Staging explicit paths does NOT keep .beads out of a worker commit. bd auto-stages .beads/issues.jsonl on any command that touches the tracker -- including read-only 'bd show' at the start of a task. So a later 'git add <explicit docs paths> && git commit' commits the ALREADY-STAGED .beads path too, silently: CLAUDE.md's 'stage explicit paths instead of git add -A' is necessary but NOT sufficient. Hit on rf2-r7nyt (PR 7595): first commit carried .beads/issues.jsonl at 2 insertions / 9 deletions -- tracker time-travel -- despite every git add naming only docs files. DETECT with 'git diff --numstat origin/main..HEAD' (compare COMMITS, not the working tree: plain 'git diff origin/main' also shows the uncommitted bd export and looks the same, so it cannot distinguish). FIX without losing the message: save it ('git log --format=%B -n 1 > msg'), 'git reset --soft origin/main', 'git restore --source=origin/main --staged .beads/issues.jsonl', re-commit -F msg, force-with-lease. Do this BEFORE any bd mutation, and never 'git checkout' .beads after a bd close. Worker worktrees have no pre-commit hook protection against this -- the installed hook guards the 90%-shrink floor, not the worker-surface boundary, unless scripts/install-git-hooks.sh has been run in the clone.

Worker worktrees can leave stale JVM processes (live-ssr, shadow-cljs server) holding ports after worktree removal. rf2-rk8gc worker hit this with port 8031 held by orphaned 'java' PID from story-deprecate-rhs worktree (long removed). Symptom: examples gate test fails to bind port. Fix: kill the stale PID. Prevention: workers should explicitly wind down long-lived background processes before exit. Worth checking ports 8030/8031/8767/9630 if examples gate fails unexpectedly with a port-binding error.

STALE .shadow-cljs CLASSPATH MIMICS THE shadow.resource UNBOUND-VAR RACE — two different causes, one identical error string (2026-07-23).

THE SYMPTOM, identical in both cases: `unbound fn: #(quote shadow.resource/slurp-resource)`, surfacing as a compile failure (seen in scripts/api-manifest/probe/).

CAUSE A — STALE CLASSPATH (benign, one-time): commit 6328dca436 changed the shadow-cljs :source-path classpath root from spec/conformance to spec/. Any worktree with a WARM .shadow-cljs still holds the old classpath.edn and fails this way after pulling that commit. CURE: delete .shadow-cljs in that worktree and recompile (1811 files, 0 warnings observed). Every warm worktree that pulls that commit needs the one-time clear — expect this across a whole wave of workers, not just one.

CAUSE B — THE REAL RACE (rf2-sff2s, recurring as rf2-drpa3.78): requiring-resolve performs its first resolve BEFORE entering the namespace require lock; shadow/resource.clj ships un-AOT-d so it compiles from source on first use, and shadow-cljs macroexpands in parallel — a thread arriving mid-load gets the interned-but-UNBOUND Var. Cured per-consumer by a namespace-local delay, and process-wide by one shared choke point that enters the serialized require path before resolving.

⚠️ WHY THIS PAIRING IS DANGEROUS: a worker fixing the race can read a stale-classpath failure as its bug reproducing, or conclude its fix failed when it actually worked. And a worker hitting the stale classpath can waste a cycle believing it found a concurrency defect.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: a shadow-cljs COMPILE failure is not reliable evidence of the race in either direction. The race must be evidenced by a CONCURRENCY PROBE in a clean Clojure process — one thread cold-loading shadow.resource, an observer resolving the same Var and reporting its state — which observes the Var directly and does not depend on any build. If clearing .shadow-cljs makes the failure vanish, it was Cause A.

MAYOR RULE: when a wave of workers is running warm worktrees and a source-path or classpath-root change lands on main, expect this error across several of them and say so in briefs; do not let it be diagnosed independently five times.

"STATE THE CONDITION, NOT THE ENUMERATION" EARNED ITS KEEP FOUR TIMES IN ONE DAY — AND THE FOURTH IS THE CLEANEST PROOF (2026-08-06, rf2-lr1rn).

THE CASE. I relayed a filing saying two rows of spec/002s tier table were affected by the new ambient-refusal exception: `override` untouched, `scope` bitten. Both were right. BUT THE SPLIT IS THREE ROWS — `hold` is touched too, because `capture-frame`s NO-ARG form resolves ambiently IN ORDER TO capture, so it refuses inside a refusing extent. (The 1-arity never consults the resolver and still carries; nothing HELD is refused — the refusal reaches the ambient capture that STARTS a hold, not the carrying that follows.)

WHY THIS IS THE CLEANEST PROOF OF THE RULE: 002s Resolver-surface section ALREADY LISTS "no-arg rf/capture-frame" among its ambient-resolving operations. So writing the CONDITION — "resolving a frame ambiently inside a refusing extent" — COVERS THE THIRD ROW FOR FREE, while the two-row ENUMERATION I relayed would have silently excluded it. The condition was not merely more durable; it was more CORRECT ON THE DAY, against a fact neither I nor the filing worker knew.

THE OTHER THREE INSTANCES TODAY, all the same shape — an enumeration under-counting its own class: an audit named 2 occurrences of a claim and there were 3 (the third in a provenance section outside the charge); a bead named 4 call sites of require-frame-provider-target! and there were 9; a pages table listed 4 verdicts against an instrument whose own docstring is headed "## The five verdicts".

AND A RELATED GOING-BEYOND-THE-BRIEF THAT WAS RIGHT: 002s "The error and its ladder" section presented a CLOSED two-way discrimination — absent target vs bad explicit target — into which a refusal fits NEITHER. Fixing only the missing tier would have left 002 telling an implementer to emit :rf.error/no-frame-context for a refused resolution. When you add a third case to a system, CHECK WHETHER SOMETHING NEARBY CLAIMS THE CASES ARE EXHAUSTIVE.

THE REASON IT STAYED SMALL, worth keeping as the test for "does this belong here?": 002s invariant is already "frame identity is carried, not found". A refusing extent is THAT INVARIANT ENFORCED STRICTLY — the refusal deletes the FINDING, never the CARRYING. So it needed a section, not an apparatus. When a new mechanism looks like it needs a home in a normative spec, ask whether it is a NEW law or an existing law applied harder; the second needs far less text.

StoryUI planning context: remember Story has an MCP surface and an associated skill. Future Story UI/spec work should treat human UI, Story MCP, and Story skill as related entry points over the same variant/plan/result/evidence substrate, not separate runtime models.

A SUBSTRATE FIX APPLIED IN ONE CONSUMER MUST BE SWEPT ACROSS EVERY CONSUMER OF THAT SUBSTRATE — rf2-8cnxg shipped in the observation port and was hit again, unfixed, in arm1's runtime (found 2026-08-07).

THE SHAPE. re-frame's observation port learned that a Reagent-hosted subscription must be ACTIVATED before it is watched — observation.cljc:1959-1982, 'ACTIVATE, then watch, then observe — and the order is the whole fix for rf2-8cnxg ... every ViewCell over a Reagent-hosted subscription rendered ONCE and never again.' Months later, arm1's Hicasso runtime attached to the same substrate with subscribe -> deref -> add-watch and NO activation, and reproduced the identical symptom. Nothing connected the two: the fix lived in the port, the bug lived in a second consumer, and no gate spanned both.

WHY IT HID SO LONG. The candidate's own bench segment installs the UIx adapter, every p0-heap row is mount-hold-release with no write, and the write-driving arms were floor/reagent/uix only. The defect needed a WRITE driven at that arm with the RATOM adapter installed — a combination the programme had never run until an allocation row demanded it. A defect that requires an untried combination of axes is invisible to every suite that varies one axis at a time.

THE RULE. When a substrate-level fix lands, grep for every OTHER site performing the same attachment sequence and check each. Under the ratom family a subscription is a bare reagent.ratom/Reaction built WITHOUT :auto-run, and a Reaction learns its sources only through deref-capture — so a plain deref outside *ratom-context* leaves 'watching' nil and the node is in nobody's watcher set. Any code that does subscribe -> deref -> add-watch without activate-derived-value! has this bug, silently, and looks like it works because it paints correctly at mount.

THE TELL, for diagnosis: stale by EVERY write since mount, not stale by one. A drain/flush fault reads stale-by-1 invariably; a never-activated reaction is deaf from birth. That arithmetic separated the two hypotheses here without running anything.

Supersede/amend an existing bead ONLY if it is OPEN and NOT in-progress and NOT closed. A dedupe/supersede match that is IN_PROGRESS (worker is mid-flight and will not see the change) or CLOSED (work is done and will not be re-actioned) must get a NEW bead instead — otherwise the new intent/work is lost. Always verify the candidate status before amending. (Mike, 2026-05-31). Generalises the rule that refinements to an in-progress bead rarely reach the worker.

SUSTAINED API 529 OUTAGE — THE MAYOR PLAYBOOK, learned 2026-07-26 when six workers were killed inside about twenty minutes.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE: task-notifications with status=failed and "API Error: 529 Overloaded", each carrying the worker last sentence — which is usually mid-diagnosis and genuinely valuable. Not stopped for cause, nothing wrong with the work.

THE MISTAKE I MADE FIRST: resuming them. SendMessage-resume during a live outage burns a worker turn and dies on contact — I resumed three and all three died again immediately, one of them twice. Resuming is correct AFTER the window, useless during it. The tell that you are still inside the window is a resumed agent failing within a minute with the same 529.

THE CORRECT POSTURE, in priority order:
1. STOP RESUMING. Each attempt costs a turn and returns nothing. The cron loop will retry; let it.
2. DO NOT DISPATCH NEW WORK. A bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface, and every new worker is another thing to recover.
3. SWITCH TO DURABILITY. Sweep every worktree: for each, compare local HEAD against git ls-remote for its branch, and count uncommitted files excluding .beads. Classify pushed / UNPUSHED / NO-REMOTE. Pushed commits survive anything; uncommitted files survive only as long as nobody reaps the worktree.
4. PROTECT THE AT-RISK ONE ON ITS BEAD. The mayor must NOT commit another worker uncommitted WIP (only that worker knows whether it forms a coherent change). But the mayor DOES control reaping — so the mitigation is to record on the bead that the worktree holds N uncommitted files, name the path and branch, and mark it EXEMPT from the hygiene loop zero-commit/clean/no-PR reap rule. That converts an invisible risk into a written one.
5. Message the still-live workers to commit and push immediately, WITH the reason — a live worker can still act even while resumes of dead ones fail.

FRESHNESS-CHECK TRAP HIT DURING THE SAME PASS, worth its own line: a find over a worktree for recently-touched files reports .beads/* churn, because bd re-exports into EVERY worktree from any worktree. Exclude .beads, .git, node_modules, .shadow-cljs and .cpcache or a cold worktree reads as warm. And even then, a count of ~4500 touched files is an npm ci or an mkdocs build, not liveness — the file COUNT is a proxy for a recent build, not for a running agent. The only reliable liveness signal remains the SendMessage response shape ("queued for delivery" = alive; "had no active task, resumed from transcript" = was idle).

AND THE THING THAT MADE THIS SURVIVABLE: push-as-you-go was already in every brief. Four of seven workers had their commits on origin and lost nothing. The one that was genuinely at risk was the one that had not committed yet. That single instruction is worth more than the entire recovery procedure.

TENTH FALSE-GREEN VARIANT: report-changed-surfaces.sh TAKES PATHS, NOT REFS, AND SILENTLY REPORTS NOTHING CHANGED (2026-07-26, hit by the scaffold-floor worker on itself).

Invoking scripts/.../report-changed-surfaces.sh origin/main treats "origin/main" as a literal FILE PATH. No such path changed, so it prints every surface false and exits successfully — i.e. "your diff touches nothing, no gate needs to run." Re-run on the real changed paths, it correctly armed examples_compile=true. There is no error, no usage message, and no hint that the argument was misread.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE INVOCATION: this is the classifier that decides which CI jobs arm. A caller who passes a ref gets a confident all-false answer, which is exactly the answer that means "skip everything". It is the same failure direction as check-beads-pr-boundary.sh exiting 0 with no base ref — a gate-adjacent script that cannot understand its input and reports the benign case rather than refusing.

DIRECTLY RELEVANT RIGHT NOW: the ci-arming worker is editing this very script to add JVM arms for tools/machines-viz and tools/testbed-support. It must pass real paths when testing its own arms, or it will see all-false and conclude its arm does not work — or worse, conclude the arm works when it has not exercised it.

GENERAL RULE, now with two instances: a script in the gate path that accepts an argument should refuse an argument it cannot interpret, not fall through to the empty result. When touching either of these, prefer making the misuse loud over documenting the correct usage.

TENTH INSTRUMENT FAULT CLASS: A LARGE-OBJECT ARM INFLATES ITS SUCCESSOR BY 2x, REPRODUCIBLY. Measuring narrow-write allocation (rf2-jr76s), an SMI control read 16.1052 B/slot in FORWARD order and 8.0027 B/slot (+0.03% against prediction) in REVERSED order — the only difference being whether an 87 KB arm ran immediately before it. No V8-level diagnosis; filed as rf2-88pie. IT WAS CAUGHT ONLY BY RUNNING BOTH ARM ORDERS, which is now standard practice on this surface and has paid for itself twice. Related large-object effect from the same run: a .slice() control calibrated to +0.56% on a small pair (100->200 doubles) but read +9.11% on a large pair (1000->10000) — V8 page-tail filler. RULE: run every measurement in both arm orders and reconcile; if one order disagrees with the other, the ARM ORDER is a variable and neither number is safe until you know why.

When testing dispatch captures via with-redefs: rf/dispatch is a MACRO that expands to rf/dispatch* (adds :rf.trace/call-site). Redef rf/dispatch* not rf/dispatch — first attempt to redef the macro lets handlers slip through. Captured opts should strip :rf.trace/call-site before assertions. Discovered in rf2-ykjl5 PR #1470 section-header affordance tests.

TEST-RUNNER FALSE GREEN: from implementation/, 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' WITHOUT '-d <dir>' makes the Cognitect runner default to a non-existent ./test and silently report 'Ran 0 tests, 0 assertions' — which READS AS GREEN. Correct form is 'clojure -M:test -d core/test -n <ns>' (adjust the -d dir per artefact). Found by the rf2-8sc64 worker on #6308, 2026-07-18. THIS AFFECTS MAYOR BRIEFS: I have repeatedly written focused-ns gate commands as 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' — any worker that ran exactly that and reported a small/zero test count may have proven nothing. When a worker reports a focused-ns run, CHECK THE TEST COUNT IS NON-ZERO and plausible for the ns; 'Ran 0 tests' or an implausibly small count is a red flag, not a pass. Prefer instructing the FULL artefact suite (clojure -M:test from the artefact dir) over a focused -n, or require the -d flag explicitly.

The 'already landed' grep has a BLIND SPOT: work fixed under a SIBLING bead's id. `git log --grep=<bead-id> origin/main` catches 'this bead was fixed and left open', but NOT 'another bead's PR captured this bead's substance'. rf2-xu6rx (interpreter memo caches -> js/Map) returned nothing for its own id, yet the swap had already merged ~12h earlier in PR #7077 under rf2-lnecd. SECOND CHECK for any bead whose body cites a finding from ANOTHER bead's report: grep the SOURCE for the change itself, not the bead id — here `grep 'js/Map' conversion.cljc` on main would have shown `#?(:cljs (js/Map.) :clj (atom {}))` already present. Rule: when a bead's provenance is 'split out of X' or 'headroom X did not capture', check whether X's own PR later captured it.

THE BASH TOOL SILENTLY STRIPS BACKSLASHES FROM HEREDOC STRINGS ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP (2026-07-26).

Found by the checker-residuals worker while probing a char-literal guard: a heredoc probe string lost its backslashes, so the probe read as a FALSE NEGATIVE — the guard looked broken when the input had been mangled before it arrived. It rewrote every probe as a FILE under its own worktree and the results reversed.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE KNOWN git worktree add BACKSLASH STRIPPING, which is already recorded, but the surface is different and more insidious: a worktree path failing is loud, whereas a mangled PROBE STRING silently changes what you are testing. Any probe involving backslashes, char literals, regex escapes or line continuations must be written to a FILE, not passed through a heredoc.

AND IT COST A REAL VERDICT IN THE SAME SESSION, in a second form: that worker plant C did not apply because of a LINE-CONTINUATION BACKSLASH in the anchor, and the self-test returned rc=0 — INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GATE THAT MISSED THE DEFECT. Only the mandated "confirm the diff applied before reading the verdict" protocol caught it. That is the twelfth false-signal class firing in the wild and being caught by the exact rule written for it.

SO THE RULE COMPOUNDS: for any mutation or probe whose payload contains a backslash, (1) write it to a file rather than a heredoc, and (2) confirm it applied by git diff --stat AND by grepping the token back out. Either check alone would have missed one of the two failures above.

A THIRD FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, unrelated but worth the same memory: a PRIME-SUFFIXED SYMBOL (db-prime, tags-prime) reads as a QUOTE to the bijection walker regex — 352 occurrences in the tree, the same class the existing backslash-quote lookbehind was written for, and a FALSE-GREEN direction. The lesson: when a regex already has a lookbehind for one lookalike, ASK WHAT ELSE LOOKS LIKE THAT — the second instance is usually already in the tree.

The core JVM suite (implementation/core clojure -M:test) runs ~10min under concurrent worker/mayor JVM load — right at the 600s foreground tool limit. This is the ROOT of the 'workers strand on backgrounded gates' pattern: a worker can't reliably foreground it when the machine is contended, so it backgrounds the gate + ends its turn with work uncommitted + no PR. THE MERGED-PR AUDIT CAN DESTRUCTIVELY OVERWRITE A BEAD'S ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (2026-07-25, found by EP-0037 review gate 2). This is a process defect in a process I do not control, and it silently destroys the only record of what a slice promised.

WHAT HAPPENED: R1's and R2's slice acceptance criteria were REWRITTEN — both the title AND the description — into the audit's follow-through text. PRs #6875/#6877 name rf2-kqxe6.5/.6 as the slice owners; their original criteria no longer exist anywhere. By contrast the audits of .3 and .7 APPENDED their findings, leaving the criteria intact. That difference is exactly why an independent completeness review could verify .3 and .7 and could NOT verify .5 and .6. Named casualty: the R2 tooling clause ended up with no bead at all.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE EPIC: acceptance criteria are the only durable record of what was promised. A merged-PR audit's job is to record what it found, and it is very good at that — it caught a keyword-as-Var false green, a load-order privacy defect, a declared-:on-* classification defect and a census extent bug. But an audit that overwrites the promise it is auditing removes the ability to check completeness later, and the loss is invisible: the bead still reads coherently, just as the audit's narrative rather than as the slice's contract.

MAYOR ACTIONS: (1) treat audit notes as APPEND-ONLY when I write them myself, and say so in briefs — findings go in notes, never over a description; (2) when a bead's description reads as audit narrative rather than as acceptance criteria, suspect this and check git history of .beads for the original; (3) rf2-twpp6 tracks the append-only repair for the two affected beads; (4) when commissioning a completeness review, tell it that a bead whose criteria were overwritten is UNVERIFIABLE and should be reported as such rather than passed — gate 2 worked this out unprompted and it is the reason its verdict is trustworthy.

GENERALISABLE FORM: any automated process that writes into the tracker can destroy the state a later reviewer needs. Prefer append. If a tool overwrites, the tracker's git history is the only recovery path — which is another reason the .beads export must keep being committed on the heartbeat.

C IS A REVIEW GAP — the fix was right and its accompanying claim was wrong, which no amount of close-reason rigour catches, because the close reason is describing a fix that IS correct. The skill↔MCP drift gate has TWO distinct failure modes — do NOT assume flake (learned 2026-07-18, rf2-92dlh). (1) The TRANSIENT flake: 'Verify skill ↔ MCP allowed-tools drift' fails under concurrent-PR load; structurally impossible when the diff has 0 skills/MCP files → --admin-justifiable. (2) A REAL main-red drift: when a PR adds/changes MCP server tools WITHOUT reconciling the consumer skills' allowed-tools + the retro drift-set, check_skill_mcp_drift.py --ci reports real findings and the gate is RED ON MAIN — every subsequent PR inherits that red. I conflated the two: rf2-vxgfnd.95.8 added 5 re-frame2-pair MCP tools (explain-render/read-view-*) without updating skills/re-frame2-pair/SKILL.md allowed-tools + scripts/check_skill_mcp_drift.py's re-frame2-pair-retro intentional_server_only set, so main's drift gate went REAL-red — and I kept --admin-ing PRs past it as 'the flake' for many merges until .95.10's spine run surfaced it (rf2-92dlh). FIX GOING FORWARD: when the drift gate is red, VERIFY main's own drift state — run/check  (or check main's gate run). If it exits non-zero (real findings), it is NOT a flake — file/dispatch a fix (allow-list the new tools in SKILL.md + the retro drift-set) instead of --admin-ing PRs past it. Only --admin when main's drift gate is GREEN and the PR's red is the load flake (0 skills/MCP diff).

A new ALWAYS-ON :rf.error/* id needs THREE co-edits in the same PR, not two: (1) the spec/009-Instrumentation.md catalogue row; (2) the Spec-Schemas.md row; (3) an entry in implementation/core/test/re_frame/error_catalogue_channel_conformance_test.clj exercise literal (~line 590) AND something that actually exercises/emits it (a register-error-listener! drive or equivalent). The test asserts parsed-always-on-set-equals-the-exercise-literal — a catalogue always-on row with no matching literal entry fails with only-in-catalogue: (:the-new-id).

⚠️ AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FLAKE HEURISTIC: I diagnosed this as a CI flake because "the diff touches 0 files under implementation/core/ and JVM core is green on main." THAT REASONING IS WRONG for cross-artefact conformance tests. The real touched surface was spec/009-Instrumentation.md (the catalogue), which the PR DID touch; a CORE test parses that shared spec file and compares it to a literal. So "diff has no core SOURCE files" does NOT imply "core gate cannot be affected" — a gate in artefact A can read a shared artefact-agnostic file (spec/009, Spec-Schemas, Conventions) that the diff edited. The flake signature must be: diff cannot affect the failing gate THROUGH ANY PATH INCLUDING SHARED SPEC FILES A GATE PARSES — not merely "no source files of that artefact in the diff." I nearly --admin-merged past a genuine touched-surface gate. The rule holds: a failing touched-surface gate is NEVER an --admin candidate; when unsure whether it is touched, READ THE FAILURE (it named the test, the file, the exact only-in-catalogue id) before concluding flake.

THE ui JVM ASSERTION COUNT IS NONDETERMINISTIC; THE TEST COUNT IS NOT. THE LOAD-BEARING TYPE MUTANT IS THE ONE THAT IS VALID IN A SIBLING CATEGORY (2026-08-06, rf2-am6qs, PR #7605).

Tightening three `:where` slots from `:any` to `:symbol`, the worker mutated four types at each slot — string, number, map, and a BARE KEYWORD. It named the keyword as the load-bearing one, and the reason is the generalisable part: OTHER CATEGORIES IN THE SAME CORPUS GENUINELY CARRY `:where :event`, `:where :flow-eval`, `:where :reactive`. So `:any` was not admitting arbitrary garbage — IT WAS ADMITTING A SPELLING THAT IS CORRECT ONE ROW OVER.

WHY THAT MATTERS FOR HOW YOU CHOOSE MUTANTS: a string/number/map mutant proves the slot rejects nonsense, which nobody was going to write. The keyword mutant proves it rejects THE MISTAKE SOMEONE WILL ACTUALLY MAKE — copying a neighbouring row. When picking negative cases for a schema slot, look for a value that is VALID IN AN ADJACENT DECLARATION and use that; the plainly-absurd mutants are the cheap ones and prove the least.

CONTROL SHAPE WORTH COPYING: each mutant had to be REJECTED by the shipped `:symbol` AND ACCEPTED by an `:any` control rebuilt from that slots OWN shipped schema, with a minimal base so only the `:where` type can be under test. Without the acceptance half you have not shown the TIGHTENING is what did the work rather than something else in the base.

AND THE CENSUS DID NOT TRANSFER, which is why it had to be redone per slot: the brief told the worker not to assume the previous slots answer carried, and the beads own call-site list was INCOMPLETE. Beyond the four sites it named there were five more through `require-frame-provider-target!` — `re-frame.freehand.substrate/frame-provider`, `v/->react`, `re-frame.ui/frame-provider` (twice, once via `require-scope-frame!`) and `re-frame.ui/->react`. A bead enumerating call sites is a starting point, never the population.

RESULT: all three tightened, no `:where` slot in Spec-Schemas.md is `:any` any more, and spec/009 needed NO edit because no row disagreed.
